note: Real-world mobility evidence for the holistic mobility scene (research:mobility, holistic views workflow). Every quote was found verbatim (whitespace, hyphenation, ligatures and typographic quotes normalized) in the copy of its source fetched on the 'accessed' date; table and feed values were compared exactly with the cached table or feed; 'check.jevSupported' is Jev's probability (TypeSafe System One, the project's 2026-gate question) that the fetched text around the quote supports 'claim' - model evidence, not proof. Matrices are lists of rows, bottom quintile first. Public figures other than Oprah Winfrey are proposals that need the author's approval.

facts.claim: In the United States, 7.5% of children with parents in the bottom income quintile reach the top quintile, compared with 11.7% in Denmark and 13.4% in Canada.
facts.unit: percent of children with bottom-fifth parents whose family income reaches the top fifth
facts.scope: United States; children born 1980-82 (9,867,736 children); parent family income averaged 1996-2000, child family income averaged 2011-12 (about age 30); national quintiles from federal income tax records
facts.quote: This probability is 7.5% in the U.S., compared with 11.7% in Denmark (Boserup, Kopczuk and Kreiner 2013) and 13.4% in Canada (Corak and Heisz 1999).
facts.notes: If parents' income played no role every cell would be 20% (paper, PDF p.28). 7.8% for the 1980-85 cohorts (Online Appendix Table VI; Tools/history/sources.json).
facts.page: PDF p.17 (printed p.16), section IV.A; Table II

check.jevClaim: In the United States, 7.5% of children with parents in the bottom income quintile reach the top quintile, compared with 11.7% in Denmark and 13.4% in Canada.

facts.claim: The chance of moving from the bottom income quintile to the top quintile is 11.7% in Denmark and 13.4% in Canada, higher than in the United States.
facts.unit: percent of children with bottom-fifth parents who reach the top fifth
facts.scope: Denmark (Boserup, Kopczuk and Kreiner 2013) and Canada (Corak and Heisz 1999), as compared with the U.S. by Chetty et al.; ranks are defined within each country
facts.quote: This probability is 7.5% in the U.S., compared with 11.7% in Denmark (Boserup, Kopczuk and Kreiner 2013) and 13.4% in Canada (Corak and Heisz 1999). In this sense, the chances of achieving the “American Dream” are considerably higher for children in Denmark and Canada than those in the U.S.
facts.notes: Secondary within Chetty et al.: the Danish and Canadian figures come from the cited studies. Within-country ranks compare relative mobility, not absolute living standards (paper, PDF p.17).

check.jevClaim: The chance of moving from the bottom income quintile to the top quintile is 11.7% in Denmark and 13.4% in Canada, higher than in the United States.

facts.claim: The probability that a child from a bottom-quintile family reaches the top quintile of the national income distribution is 4.4% in Charlotte and 12.9% in San Jose.

facts.scope: commuting zones where the children grew up; children born 1980-85 (Table III column 5); national quintiles
facts.quote: the probability that a child reaches the top quintile of the national income distribution starting from a family in the bottom quintile is 4.4% in Charlotte but 12.9% in San Jose.
facts.notes: The paper adds that San Jose's chances 'are comparable to those in Denmark and Canada' (PDF p.28).
facts.page: PDF p.1 (abstract); Table III, PDF p.71

check.jevClaim: The probability that a child from a bottom-quintile family reaches the top quintile of the national income distribution is 4.4% in Charlotte and 12.9% in San Jose.

facts.claim: In Table III, the probability that a child with bottom-quintile parents reaches the top quintile is 10.8% in Salt Lake City, 12.9% in San Jose, 10.5% in Boston, 12.2% in San Francisco, 10.5% in New York, 9.6% in Los Angeles, 11.0% in Washington DC, 10.9% in Seattle, 9.3% in Houston, 6.5% in Chicago, 4.5% in Milwaukee, 5.5% in Detroit, 4.5% in Atlanta and 4.4% in Charlotte.

facts.notes: Row layout: rank, CZ, population, absolute upward mobility (expected rank at parent percentile 25), P(Q5|Q1) in percent, percent above poverty line, rank-rank slope. The table's notes say column 5 uses the 1980-85 cohorts; the other columns use 1980-82.

check.jevClaim: In Table III, the probability that a child with bottom-quintile parents reaches the top quintile is 10.8% in Salt Lake City, 12.9% in San Jose, 10.5% in Boston, 12.2% in San Francisco, 10.5% in New York, 9.6% in Los Angeles, 11.0% in Washington DC, 10.9% in Seattle, 9.3% in Houston, 6.5% in Chicago, 4.5% in Milwaukee, 5.5% in Detroit, 4.5% in Atlanta and 4.4% in Charlotte.

facts.claim: Among the 50 largest U.S. commuting zones, absolute upward mobility (the mean rank of children with parents at the 25th percentile) ranges from 35.8 in Charlotte to 46.2 in Salt Lake City.

check.jevClaim: Among the 50 largest U.S. commuting zones, absolute upward mobility (the mean rank of children with parents at the 25th percentile) ranges from 35.8 in Charlotte to 46.2 in Salt Lake City.

facts.claim: In the United States, a one percentile increase in parents' income rank is associated with a 0.341 percentile increase in their child's mean income rank.
facts.unit: percentile-rank points of child income per percentile-rank point of parent income (rank-rank slope)
facts.scope: United States; children born 1980-82; family income ranks
facts.quote: we estimate that a one percentage point (pp) increase in parent rank is associated with a 0.341 pp increase in the child’s mean rank
facts.notes: Standard error 0.0003. The gap between children of the richest and poorest parents is about 34 percentiles (100 x slope). 0.323 for the 1980-85 cohorts (Table I column 6).
facts.page: PDF p.16 (printed p.15); Table I row 4

check.jevClaim: In the United States, a one percentile increase in parents' income rank is associated with a 0.341 percentile increase in their child's mean income rank.

facts.unit: rank-rank slope

facts.quote: The rank-rank slope is 0.180 in Denmark and 0.174 in Canada, nearly half that in the U.S.

check.jevClaim: The rank-rank slope is 0.180 in Denmark and 0.174 in Canada, about half of the U.S. value.

facts.quote: Under the benchmark of copula stability, the fraction of children earning more than their parents fell from 92% in the 1940 birth cohort to 50% in the 1984 birth cohort.
facts.notes: Abstract rounds this to 'approximately 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s'. The 1940 value is bounded between 84% and 98% across plausible copulas (Tools/history/sources.json).
facts.page: PDF p.4 (introduction); Figure 1B text PDF p.11

check.jevClaim: The fraction of U.S. children who earn more than their parents fell from 92% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in 1984.

facts.claim: Share of each U.S. birth cohort earning more than their parents at 30, 1940-1984.
facts.unit: percent of children earning more than their parents at age 30 (cohort mean; cohort_mean x 100, one decimal)
facts.scope: United States birth cohorts 1940-1984 (every cohort is in the table; five-year steps shown here)
facts.quote: cohort_mean: Mean probability for a child from a given birth cohort to earn more than their parents (codebook); values read in the table's cohort_mean column
facts.notes: Read from the xlsx (converted to TSV by a stdlib reader) and compared value by value by the builder; the codebook (Online-Table-1-Readme.pdf) defines cohort_mean as the 'Mean probability for a child from a given birth cohort to earn more than their parents'. 1940 (0.915) and 1984 (0.503) round to the paper's 92% and 50%. The 1980 cohort's 0.500 is the series minimum.

facts.claim: Share earning more than their parents by parents' income percentile, 1940 and 1984 cohorts.
facts.unit: percent of children earning more than their parents at age 30, by parents' income percentile
facts.scope: United States birth cohorts 1940 and 1984
facts.quote: Rates of absolute mobility fell the most for children with parents in the middle class. (paper, PDF p.4); values read in the table's abs_mob_pos_par_p10/p50/p90 columns
facts.notes: The paper: 'Rates of absolute mobility fell the most for children with parents in the middle class' (PDF p.4). Children of top-decile parents fall furthest in percentage points here too, but for them earning less than rich parents is the expected regression.

facts.claim: Among children with parents in the bottom income quintile, 10.6% of white children reach the top quintile compared with 2.5% of Black children.
facts.unit: percent of children with bottom-fifth parents whose household income reaches the top fifth
facts.scope: United States; children born 1978-83 in the U.S. (or authorized child immigrants), about 20 million; child household income averaged 2014-15 (ages 31-37); parent household income 1994-95 and 1998-2000
facts.quote: among children with parents in the bottom quintile, 10.6% of white children rise up to the top quintile, but only 2.5% of black children do
facts.notes: The non-technical summary (alsoQuoted) states the same in plain words.

alsoQuoted.quote: black children born to parents in the bottom household income quintile have a 2.5% chance of rising to the top quintile of household income, compared with 10.6% for whites.

check.jevClaim: Among children with parents in the bottom income quintile, 10.6% of white children reach the top quintile compared with 2.5% of Black children.

facts.claim: Among children with top-quintile parents, 41.1% of white children and 18.0% of Black children stay in the top quintile, and 16.7% of Black children fall to the bottom quintile.
facts.unit: percent of children with top-fifth parents
facts.scope: same sample as chjp2018-q1-to-q5-by-race
facts.quote: Among children with parents in the top quintile, 41.1% of white children remain in the top quintile, compared with 18.0% of black children. Perhaps most strikingly, black children starting from families in the top quintile have nearly the same chances of falling to the bottom income quintile (16.7%) as they do of staying in the top quintile.
facts.notes: The summary's plain-language version is in alsoQuoted.

alsoQuoted.quote: Black children born to parents in the top income quintile are almost as likely to fall to the bottom quintile as they are to remain in the top quintile. By contrast, white children born in the top quintile are nearly five times as likely to stay there as they are to fall to the bottom.

check.jevClaim: Among children with top-quintile parents, 41.1% of white children and 18.0% of Black children stay in the top quintile, and 16.7% of Black children fall to the bottom quintile.

facts.claim: Controlling for parental income, Black boys have lower incomes in adulthood than white boys in 99% of Census tracts.
facts.unit: percent of Census tracts in which Black boys have lower adult incomes than white boys raised at the same parental income
facts.scope: boys with parents at the 25th percentile; children born 1978-83
facts.quote: Controlling for parental income, black boys have lower incomes in adulthood than white boys in 99% of Census tracts.
facts.notes: The paper finds the gap is driven by men's outcomes; Black and white women raised at the same parental income have similar individual incomes (summary, Finding 2).

check.jevClaim: Controlling for parental income, Black boys have lower incomes in adulthood than white boys in 99% of Census tracts.

facts.claim: Between the 1978 and 1992 birth cohorts, earnings gaps by parental income among white children grew by 30%, while white-Black earnings gaps for children from low-income families shrank by 30%.
facts.unit: percent change in the earnings gap between the 1978 and 1992 birth cohorts
facts.scope: United States birth cohorts 1978-1992; Census and tax data
facts.quote: Between the 1978 and 1992 birth cohorts, earnings increased for white children from high-income families relative to white children from low-income families, increasing earnings gaps by parental income (“class”) by 30%. Earnings increased for Black children at all parental income levels, reducing white-Black earnings gaps for children from low-income families by 30%.
facts.notes: A working paper (not yet peer reviewed, per the NBER notice), revised December 2025. It updates the 2018 race facts: the race gap has been shrinking while class gaps among white children grew; the authors attribute both to changes in parental employment rates in children's local communities.

check.jevClaim: Between the 1978 and 1992 birth cohorts, earnings gaps by parental income among white children grew by 30%, while white-Black earnings gaps for children from low-income families shrank by 30%.

facts.claim: In an average OECD country it would take around four to five generations for children from the bottom earnings decile to reach mean earnings.
facts.unit: generations for the offspring of a bottom-10% family to reach mean income (OECD24 average; 'four to five')
facts.scope: 24 OECD countries with comparable father-son earnings elasticities; simulation assuming constant elasticities (Bowles and Gintis 2002)
facts.quote: As a result, in an “average OECD country” it would take around four to five generations for children from the bottom earnings decile to attain the level of mean earnings.
facts.notes: Figure 1.5 note: 'These estimates are simulation-based and intended to be illustrative.' 4.5 is the OECD24 point in the figure's StatLink data (oecd2018-generations-by-country).

check.jevClaim: In an average OECD country it would take around four to five generations for children from the bottom earnings decile to reach mean earnings.

facts.claim: Expected generations for a bottom-10% family's offspring to reach mean income, by country.
facts.unit: expected number of generations for the offspring of a bottom-10% family to reach the mean income
facts.scope: OECD and emerging economies, as published June 2018
facts.quote: Expected number of generations it would take the offspring from a family at the bottom 10% to reach the mean income in society [...] Denmark	DNK	2 [...] United States	USA	5 [...] Colombia	COL	11
facts.notes: Every row is compared with the StatLink file by the builder. Caution: the overview's prose (printed p.26) says the Nordic countries take 'at least four generations - more than 100 years', which contradicts this figure and the executive summary ('only about two generations ... in the Nordic countries', printed p.16). Use the figure's data; do not quote that sentence.

facts.claim: Intergenerational earnings mobility and the Gini coefficient by country (OECD Figure 1.13).
facts.unit: mobility = 1 minus the father-son intergenerational earnings elasticity; gini = Gini coefficient of income, mid-1980s/early 1990s (both 0-1, rounded to 3 decimals)
facts.scope: 24 OECD countries, the OECD24 average and 6 emerging economies (ISO 3166 alpha-3 codes, as in the file)
facts.quote: Figure 1.13. In most countries, earnings mobility across generations is higher when income inequality is lower [...] Note: Earnings mobility is proxied by 1 minus the intergenerational earnings elasticity of fathers with sons. Gini coefficients refer to the mid-1980s/early 1990s.
facts.notes: Both axes of a Great Gatsby Curve from one source. Its U.S. elasticity (1 - 0.590 = 0.41) differs from Corak's 0.47 (corak-ige-by-country): different underlying studies, so never mix the two series in one picture. The overview adds that Hungary, France, Germany and Austria combine lower inequality with lower mobility, and that 'there are no countries which combine high inequality with high mobility' (printed p.35).

facts.claim: Intergenerational earnings elasticity between fathers and sons in 22 countries (Corak).
facts.unit: intergenerational earnings elasticity between fathers' and sons' earnings (share of a father's earnings advantage passed to his son)
facts.scope: 22 countries; published estimates collected by Corak with the methods of Corak (2006); sons born roughly in the early to mid 1960s
facts.quote: Comparable estimates of the intergenerational elasticity between father and son earnings for the United States and twenty one other countries [...] United States .47 [...] Denmark .15 [...] Peru .67 [...] the intergenerational earnings elasticity of 0.47 in the United States is more than twice as high as the Canadian estimate of roughly 0.20
facts.notes: Every bar label is compared with the paper's text by the builder. These are the vertical axis of Krueger's Great Gatsby Curve. Values are point estimates from different studies made comparable; treat as approximate.

facts.claim: In Finland, Norway and Denmark less than one-fifth of a father's economic advantage or disadvantage is passed on to his son, while in Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States roughly 50 percent is passed on.
facts.unit: share of a father's economic advantage or disadvantage passed on to his son in adulthood
facts.scope: sons born roughly in the early to mid 1960s, adult outcomes in the mid to late 1990s
facts.quote: In countries like Finland, Norway, and Denmark the tie between parental economic status and the adult earnings of children is weakest: less than one-fifth of any economic advantage or disadvantage that a father may have had in his time is passed on to a son in adulthood. In Italy, the United Kingdom, and the United States roughly 50 percent of any advantage or disadvantage is passed on.
facts.notes: Plain-language reading of the elasticity for captions.

check.jevClaim: In Finland, Norway and Denmark less than one-fifth of a father's economic advantage or disadvantage is passed on to his son, while in Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States roughly 50 percent is passed on.

facts.claim: On 12 January 2012 Alan Krueger named the relationship between inequality and intergenerational persistence the Great Gatsby Curve and predicted that the U.S. intergenerational earnings elasticity would rise from .47 to .56.
facts.unit: intergenerational earnings elasticity
facts.scope: United States; projection for the next generation from the cross-country inequality-mobility relationship and the rise in U.S. inequality over the previous 25 years
facts.quote: I call this the “Great Gatsby Curve.” [...] The IGE for the U.S. is predicted to rise from .47 to .56. In other words, the persistence in the advantages and disadvantages of income passed from parents to the children is predicted to rise by about a quarter for the next generation as a result of the rise in inequality that the U.S. has seen in the last 25 years.
facts.notes: Dated 12 January 2012, the first public use of the name (Corak 2013: Krueger 'used this label for the first time' in this speech). The projection is a rough forecast, not a measurement; Chetty et al. (2014, AER P&P) later found the rank-rank slope roughly stable for cohorts born 1971-1993 (Tools/history/sources.json chettyEtAl2014Trend).

check.jevClaim: On 12 January 2012 Alan Krueger named the relationship between inequality and intergenerational persistence the Great Gatsby Curve and predicted that the U.S. intergenerational earnings elasticity would rise from .47 to .56.

facts.claim: About half of the taxpayers in the bottom income quintile in 1996 had moved to a higher income group by 2005: 58 percent by one measure and 45 percent by another.
facts.unit: percent of taxpayers in the bottom income quintile in 1996 who were in a higher quintile in 2005
